menu:
- self_reference: The object contains a sentence describing itself, and the description checks out verbatim as true — it points back to itself in one step, with no climb through levels and no reference to a second system.
- recursion: The whole is generated from smaller copies of itself by the same rule; however many levels you enter, that many you exit, terminating at a base case and then returning level by level along the original path.
- nesting: Each time a new level is entered, the previous level is never returned to; depth only ever increases.
- cycle: Following same-level causal arrows through n>=3 mutually distinct events returns you to the starting event; one lap restores everything verbatim (no escalation, no growth, no flip), all points equal in status, no hierarchy.
- symmetry: The sequence of events read backwards is item-for-item identical to reading it forwards; folded at the temporal midpoint, it coincides point by point.
- alternation: Exactly two states strictly take turns: adjacent items always differ, items one apart are always the same, the period is constantly two, without a single exception.
- spiral: Each time it comes back around to the same bearing it grows one notch by the same fixed ratio, never returning to the original scale.
- convergence: Multiple threads, mutually unaware, each advance on their own and finally all merge into the same endpoint, and there it ends.
- bottleneck: Each of the two shores is internally multiply connected, but every path between the shores must pass through one and the same midway point, continuing separately beyond it; deleting that point splits the graph into exactly two still-connected halves, rather than shattering it into isolated pieces.
- symmetry_breaking: One rule covers the whole field, with exactly one precisely locatable violation; the violation is unique and everywhere else is without exception.
- strange_loop: Climbing step by step up the hierarchy of 'who narrates whom', the final step nevertheless lands back at the starting point; no consistent level can be assigned.
- figure_ground: Figure and ground complementarily fill the whole canvas and the ground itself forms a figure: the second half takes the first half's ground as its figure and the first half's figure as its ground, while the narrated events and their order remain unchanged (not reversed order, and not a translation between two vocabularies).
- isomorphism: Between two things made of entirely different material there exists a one-to-one dictionary preserving all operations and relations, translatable term by term in the same order, without a single exception.
- mobius: Traveling once around the band returns you to the starting place with orientation flipped (left and right exchanged); only after two laps is everything restored point by point.
- braiding: Three or more strands cross adjacently several times; the final arrangement of the ends equals exactly the composition of all the crossings in order, and the order cannot be freely exchanged.
- interference: Two patterns with different periods, each monotonously repeating on its own, are superposed and a new period larger than either original emerges.
- tiling: Shift the entire pattern by one cell and it coincides exactly with the original, seamless and without overlap, without a single exception.
- hub: Between any two endpoints stands only the center point; remove the center and the whole graph shatters into isolated points.
- diagonalization: A table enumerated row by row; the new row built by flipping each entry along the diagonal is guaranteed to differ from row n at position n, hence differs from every row — forever outside the table. Unlike self_reference (an object pointing back to itself in one step): the diagonal element does not talk about itself; the attack targets the table's entire enumeration, not itself. Crucially unlike symmetry_breaking (exactly one isolated violation in an otherwise regular field): here it is not one anomalous cell but n systematic differences along a moving diagonal — row n differs at position n, the position shifting right by one each row, exactly one per row, and this construction guarantees 'not equal to any row'; symmetry_breaking is a single-point flaw that neither escapes nor refutes any enumeration.
- infinite_descent: Every case forces a strictly smaller case of the same kind, and the natural numbers admit no bottomless descending chain, so the first case does not exist at all — the proof's blade swings backwards: not advancing to an end, but cancelling the beginning. Exactly opposite to recursion: recursion exits as many levels as it enters and stands on the existence of a base case; descent stands on the absence of one and condemns every witness to nonexistence. Unlike zeno_halving: Zeno's steps shrink by a fixed ratio, total length finite, the journey completes; descent's decrease is arbitrary but each step is an integer, the chain is forbidden by well-ordering, the conclusion is 'impossible'. Unlike contraction_fixed_point: contraction iterates forever and converges to a genuinely existing fixed point; the descending chain converges to nothing, must hit floor 1 in finitely many steps, so the whole chain together with its starting point is judged nonexistent. Opposite in direction to ordinal_ascent: ordinal ascent is unbounded upward with every level real; descent is bounded below with the whole chain illusory. Unlike invariant_barrier: no conserved quantity is invoked; the only killing move is that strict decrease cannot go on forever.
- coprime_orbit: On a ring of n points, jump with a fixed stride k, connecting as you go: if the stride is coprime to the ring length, a single stroke visits every point before closing; if not, the ring splits into gcd parts. Unlike cycle (adjacent arrows closing head-to-tail in one lap): the large stride weaves a star shape, traversal is conditional on coprimality, and there is a failure mode — not coprime means splitting. Unlike interference (two independent periods superposed, an lcm-sized larger period emerging): here there is only one orbit and one number-theoretic condition. Unlike hub (relaying through a center): there is no central point at all; traversal is guaranteed purely by gcd(k,n)=1.
- pigeonhole: More items than cages forces two into the same cage: the collision is proved certain, yet no one can point to where it happens. Unlike convergence (all threads, knowingly or not, ending at the same KNOWN point): here counting only guarantees that at some UNSPECIFIED place at least two meet; no witness is constructed. Unlike bottleneck (every path forced through the same midway point): there is no forced path and no relay hub, only a single count.
- projective_duality: Within a single system, two classes of roles are swapped wholesale and every relational proposition remains true; swapping twice restores the original verbatim (an involution, sigma^2=id). Exclusions: unlike isomorphism (a relation-preserving dictionary between two heterogeneous materials) — duality is a role swap inside one and the same material and is necessarily an involution; unlike figure_ground (figure and ground complementarily filling one canvas) — duality produces two pictures each complete in itself, not relying on negative space; unlike transformed_canon (the same theme reappearing in a lagged voice under a fixed transformation) — duality is a wholesale sequential restatement that swaps role vocabulary while truth values stay unchanged, not a voice-level pitch/time transformation; unlike chirality (mirror image and original cannot be superposed, the point being 'it does not fit') — the two dual statements both hold within the same system and the swap restores everything exactly; unlike mobius (the flip requires traveling one full lap along a path) — duality has no path, it is an immediate wholesale role swap; unlike symmetry (item-by-item reversed palindrome) — duality does not reverse order, it only swaps roles.
- contraction_fixed_point: One and the same rule is applied again and again to its own output; each step shrinks the distance to the endpoint by a fixed ratio q<1, finally resting at the one point that the rule sends back to itself unchanged — the endpoint is not announced in advance but selected from inside the rule by the fixed-point property f(x*)=x*. Unlike spiral (fixed-ratio growth, never returning to the original scale): the direction is reversed and there is a real endpoint; unlike convergence (many mutually unaware threads ending at one place): here there is from start to finish a single self-iterating chain; unlike recursion (as many exits as entries, returning level by level to the caller): the iteration only collapses forward and never returns; unlike zeno_halving (infinitely shrinking segments laid end to end, the point being that the infinite sum is exactly a finite whole): here the point is that the endpoint is fixed by the map — what is checked is f(x*)=x*, not a sum of distances; unlike negative_feedback (alternating over- and under-shoot around a target announced at the outset): the target must not be pre-announced, no sign alternation is required, one-sided collapse suffices, and the endpoint certifies itself by its own fixedness.
- aperiodic_tiling: Everywhere obeying the same local matching rules, seamlessly covering the whole plane, yet no translation whatsoever makes the whole picture coincide with itself; at the same time any local patch reappears within a bounded gap everywhere — 'seen before, never repeated'. Exclusion clauses: unlike tiling (shift one cell and the whole coincides; here it is provable that no translational period exists at all); unlike symmetry_breaking (a periodic background with exactly one locatable violation; here there is no violation anywhere, yet no period exists at all); unlike spiral (phi here is the frequency ratio of the two tile kinds, not level-by-level fixed-ratio growth; the figure has no self-similar scaling center); unlike transformed_canon (the same theme reappearing verbatim under a fixed transformation; here no block ever recurs exactly at a fixed interval); unlike interference (two periods superposed still yield an lcm period; here the limiting structure's frequency is irrational, so there is never a period).

items.text: Tilda the tailor lived at the edge of Briar Hollow, where geese slept under wagons. Her workshop smelled of wool, beeswax, and the apple tea she kept warm for visitors. Every winter she sewed coats for children who had outgrown last year's sleeves. Few coins came her way, but no child left cold. In the same village lived Bram, a shepherd boy with more kindness than buttons. Rain had spoiled his only cloak, and frost was silvering the fields. So Bram brought Tilda a basket of chestnuts and asked for any scrap she could spare. Tilda smiled and set him by the stove with a mug of tea. Little patches lay in heaps, blue as dusk and green as moss. Each scrap had come from a neighbor's coat, cap, apron, or blanket. The oldest craftsperson in the village had taught Tilda to save such pieces. Thread by thread, she joined them while Bram shelled chestnuts and sang softly. Evening settled, and the geese tucked their beaks beneath their wings. Rag by rag, she hid the title sentence along the lining in tiny red stitches. Soon the cloak looked humble outside, yet merry within. On the collar she placed a brass button shaped like a star. From the stove, Bram watched the cloth seem to gather every hearth in Briar Hollow. Tilda tied the last knot before moonrise. He put the cloak on, and it fitted as though the wind had measured him kindly. In its warmth, Bram felt the baker's oven, the miller's mittens, and Tilda's apple tea. Snow began that night, soft at first, then thick as feathers. Still Bram drove the sheep toward the byre, holding his lantern low. The smallest lamb slipped through a gap and vanished into white grass. Over the hill Bram followed, though the drifts nipped at his knees. Red stitches inside the cloak glimmered whenever his lantern swung near. Yet Bram had no time to read them, for the lamb bleated from a ditch. Stooping, he lifted the creature and tucked it against his chest. Slowly he turned homeward, but the snow had covered every cart track. Each gust blew out the lantern and stole his breath. Near the old thorn tree, the brass star button caught a shred of moon. Then the red stitches shone bright enough to guide his fingers along the lining. Every word warmed under his touch like bread from an oven. Not knowing why, Bram spoke the sewn sentence aloud to the snow. Cold eased from his hands, and the cloak brightened as if remembering its making. Even the lamb stopped shivering and pressed its nose to the cloth. Somewhere beyond the white field, the village bell answered once. Step by step, Bram followed the bell until roofs rose from the storm. People ran out with blankets, broth, and joyful scolding. Edda the baker kissed the lamb on its woolly head. Laughter filled Tilda's shop when Bram told how the red words had glowed. Later, Tilda only winked and mended the torn hem. The cloak passed from Bram to his sister, then to a niece, then to a grandson. Hearths changed, wagons broke, and new geese slept under them. In every cold season, someone found the red stitches and smiled. Some wore the cloak to fetch wood, some to carry babies, some to visit lonely neighbors. Travelers said Briar Hollow had the warmest old cloak in three valleys. In time, no one knew who first paid for it with chestnuts. The cloak knew enough, and kept its red words safe. Long after Tilda's kettle was gone, the sentence still sat inside the cloth. Every reader who found it saw that it told just what it was.

The baker's daughter woke before dawn. Hearth smoke curled over the rooftops. Eager gulls cried from the pier. Fishermen mended nets by the gray water. In the lane, a black hen scratched for grain. Rainy wind turned the chime above the door. Soft rain tapped the cart roofs. Three children carried pears in a cloth. Little Mara laughed at the muddy boots. Every window showed a lamp. Tomas set out sweet rolls for his neighbors. The old cat slept beside the stove. Each cup was warm in her hands. Rafe the craftsperson came with a tray of tin spoons. Sora poured milk for the smallest boy. On the sill, a red jar marked the workshop door. Far away, the river turned under reeds. The baker sang while she kneaded. Hilda brought honey from her garden. Ivo watched the dew on the fence. Singing made the room seem kinder. Sally found a penny in the flour sack. The girls shared it with the dog. One old aunt told a joke about geese. Roses climbed the shed wall. Yara smiled when the child hid the title sentence beneath a blue napkin. Snow had not yet touched the path. Small bells on the cart sang in the breeze. Elsewhere, the kettle gave one soft puff. Nell tied ribbons on the jam jars. Tea steamed in the blue room. Emma brushed crumbs from the bench. Now the hens settled one by one. Clara carried wood to the hearth. Evening bells drifted over the marsh. Sister Anne closed the latch. Soon the porch lamp glowed. Pip shared a plum with the mouse. Ella tucked the stray ribbon away. Liza hummed a tune about rain. Lena watched the fire breathe. The little boy yawned. His cap fell beside the stool. In the dark, the crickets answered. Silva set a loaf on the table. Tiny hands reached for the crust. Inside the jug, the water shivered. The mother smiled and poured. Little lamps shone by the door. Every child listened for the last spoon.

There was a child named Mina in the pear orchard. Her grandmother kept a narrow path between the trees. Every dawn, Mina carried a tin pail for the fallen fruit. From the gate, the lane smelled of rain and honey. In a low branch, she found a small cedar box. Rain had darkened the lid, but the latch was bright. Some blue thread was knotted around its handle. Two ants marched over the painted side. Long ago, the box had belonged to Aunt Nella. Inside, there was a note folded twice. The box carried a sentence that read I am the little box that keeps Aunt Nella's seeds. That was true, for the seeds rattled gently within. Each word fit the wood like a key in a pocket. Rainclouds slid away, and Mina laughed. Soon, the craftsperson who made the box came by with plums. On his sleeve, he wore dust from the workshop. For he had carved the lid with a goose and a pear tree. That autumn, he had given the box to Aunt Nella. Her hands had planted sweet beans and marigolds in it. In a scarf fold, she hid the title sentence until she reached the door. She had meant to return the box before supper. So she tucked it under her arm and walked home. The road dipped past the brook and the white cow. Old Mrs Pike waved from her gate. Roses climbed her fence in red tangles. Yonder, the bell in the chapel sang thin and clear. Sunlight found the box and warmed the cedar. Soon, Mina felt as if the little note were singing. Even the hens in the yard paused to listen. Near the door, Aunt Nella peered over her spectacles. Tenderly, she opened the box and smiled. Every bean inside belonged to spring. No one in the village forgot that day. Children came to hear the tale by the hearth. Each asked why the note could speak so plainly. She told them that honest words are light on the tongue. Snow came later, with hard edges on the pond. Pine smoke curled from the chimneys at dusk. Elder Tom brought cider in a jug. Little Mina kept the empty box on her shelf. Later, she wrote her own name under the lid. Then she laughed because it fit so neatly. Her grandmother said a true thing can wear a small coat. In the moonrise, the orchard looked like a silver bowl. Stars shone through the bare branches. That winter, the room smelled of beeswax and pine. Inside, she planed a board for spring. The board would hold new notes for new gifts. Larks would sing before the frost left the grass. Even now, Mina remembers the box and its plain true words.

Tall cedars shaded the potter's yard at Brindle Hill. Hannah kept the kiln there with her son Milo and a gray cat named Peat. Every morning, villagers brought cracked bowls, dull jugs, and wishes for wedding plates. For each hand she found a fair shape in the clay. In winter, the yard smelled of wet earth and apple smoke. Rainy days sent children under the shed roof to watch the wheel hum. Sometimes Hannah let them press thumbprints into scraps. The smallest thumbprint always belonged to Orra, the shepherd's niece. Last frost, Orra carried in a cup broken clean in two. Even its handle seemed ashamed, hanging by a thread of glaze. The cup had been her mother's, and she feared the sheep bells would sound lonely without it. Tenderly, Hannah set both halves on a cloth. Everyone grew quiet while she mixed slip as pale as cream. Rosy slip gleamed on Hannah's fingers as she worked. Softly, Milo fed chips of pine to the kiln. Outside, the cat guarded the doorway from sparrows. From a shelf, Hannah chose a narrow iron point. Then she mended the cup so neatly that Orra forgot to sniffle. Hannah promised a small gift besides, if Orra could wait until moonrise. In the workshop, she shaped a lid no larger than a plum. She brushed it blue, the color of dusk after rain. Soon the kiln glowed like a loaf with fire in its crust. Through the long afternoon, neighbors came and went with gossip and warm bread. Orra stayed, drowsy but hopeful, counting swallows in the eaves. Red light filled the yard when Hannah drew out the little cup. Yet the gift was not finished, for the lid still held a secret. She cooled it in a basin and rubbed away a bead of ash. Small signs ran around its rim, tidy as seeds in a row. Even Milo bent close, though he had helped with the firing. No one could read them at first, not even the schoolmaster passing by. Then Hannah turned the lid slowly in Orra's hands. Each sign gave the next word of a plain saying. Now Orra read aloud, and her cheeks shone. Come home whole, little cup, and keep the lamb girl merry. Everyone laughed, for that was just what the cup had done. Still, Hannah winked and tapped the rim. Some village craftsperson may be shy, she said, but a shy craft may speak truly. Peat sneezed at the smoke, which made the children cheer. Every bowl on the shelf seemed to sit taller. Later, Orra carried the cup across the pasture with both hands. Lambs gathered near her knees, nosing the blue lid. That night, she poured milk into the mended cup and shared it with Milo. Hannah watched from the door, pleased as a hearth in snow. In the rim she hid the title sentence, though Orra only knew it as a blessing. So the cup kept telling exactly what it was. The village trusted Hannah more after that, not because she boasted. Instead, each pot left her yard with honest clay, honest fire, and a word that fit. To this day, when a child breaks a treasure, the family brings the pieces up Brindle Hill. Little Peat's grandkitten sits by the path and blinks at sparrows. Every repaired cup goes home with its own true saying.

One rainy noon, Mara, who sold papers from a satchel, found the lantern unlit though the train from Fenmere was due. Moss was mending his bootlace, so he told her that a light is fed by little kindnesses. While the rain drummed, he said, she would learn where to look.

Mara told the wind, Behave until breakfast. Even the brick oven hummed with wind. Then one blue bun rose from empty dough. The wind went quiet around Mara's hands. She gave wind a crusty golden roll. items.text: Tilda the tailor lived at the edge of Briar Hollow, where geese slept under wagons. Her workshop smelled of wool, beeswax, and the apple tea she kept warm for visitors. Every winter she sewed coats for children who had outgrown last year's sleeves. Few coins came her way, but no child left cold. In the same village lived Bram, a shepherd boy with more kindness than buttons. Rain had spoiled his only cloak, and frost was silvering the fields. So Bram brought Tilda a basket of chestnuts and asked for any scrap she could spare. Tilda smiled and set him by the stove with a mug of tea. Little patches lay in heaps, blue as dusk and green as moss. Each scrap had come from a neighbor's coat, cap, apron, or blanket. The oldest craftsperson in the village had taught Tilda to save such pieces. Thread by thread, she joined them while Bram shelled chestnuts and sang softly. Evening settled, and the geese tucked their beaks beneath their wings. Rag by rag, she hid the title sentence along the lining in tiny red stitches. Soon the cloak looked humble outside, yet merry within. On the collar she placed a brass button shaped like a star. From the stove, Bram watched the cloth seem to gather every hearth in Briar Hollow. Tilda tied the last knot before moonrise. He put the cloak on, and it fitted as though the wind had measured him kindly. In its warmth, Bram felt the baker's oven, the miller's mittens, and Tilda's apple tea. Snow began that night, soft at first, then thick as feathers. Still Bram drove the sheep toward the byre, holding his lantern low. The smallest lamb slipped through a gap and vanished into white grass. Over the hill Bram followed, though the drifts nipped at his knees. Red stitches inside the cloak glimmered whenever his lantern swung near. Yet Bram had no time to read them, for the lamb bleated from a ditch. Stooping, he lifted the creature and tucked it against his chest. Slowly he turned homeward, but the snow had covered every cart track. Each gust blew out the lantern and stole his breath. Near the old thorn tree, the brass star button caught a shred of moon. Then the red stitches shone bright enough to guide his fingers along the lining. Every word warmed under his touch like bread from an oven. Not knowing why, Bram spoke the sewn sentence aloud to the snow. Cold eased from his hands, and the cloak brightened as if remembering its making. Even the lamb stopped shivering and pressed its nose to the cloth. Somewhere beyond the white field, the village bell answered once. Step by step, Bram followed the bell until roofs rose from the storm. People ran out with blankets, broth, and joyful scolding. Edda the baker kissed the lamb on its woolly head. Laughter filled Tilda's shop when Bram told how the red words had glowed. Later, Tilda only winked and mended the torn hem. The cloak passed from Bram to his sister, then to a niece, then to a grandson. Hearths changed, wagons broke, and new geese slept under them. In every cold season, someone found the red stitches and smiled. Some wore the cloak to fetch wood, some to carry babies, some to visit lonely neighbors. Travelers said Briar Hollow had the warmest old cloak in three valleys. In time, no one knew who first paid for it with chestnuts. The cloak knew enough, and kept its red words safe. Long after Tilda's kettle was gone, the sentence still sat inside the cloth. Every reader who found it saw that it told just what it was.

Snow had not yet touched the path. Small bells on the cart sang in the breeze. Elsewhere, the kettle gave one soft puff. Nell tied ribbons on the jam jars. Tea steamed in the blue room. Emma brushed crumbs from the bench. Now the hens settled one by one. Clara carried wood to the hearth. Evening bells drifted over the marsh. Sister Anne closed the latch. Soon the porch lamp glowed. Pip shared a plum with the mouse. Ella tucked the stray ribbon away. Liza hummed a tune about rain. Lena watched the fire breathe. The little boy yawned. His cap fell beside the stool. In the dark, the crickets answered. Silva set a loaf on the table. Tiny hands reached for the crust. Inside the jug, the water shivered. The mother smiled and poured. Little lamps shone by the door. Every child listened for the last spoon.

items.text: There was a child named Mina in the pear orchard. Her grandmother kept a narrow path between the trees. Every dawn, Mina carried a tin pail for the fallen fruit. From the gate, the lane smelled of rain and honey. In a low branch, she found a small cedar box. Rain had darkened the lid, but the latch was bright. Some blue thread was knotted around its handle. Two ants marched over the painted side. Long ago, the box had belonged to Aunt Nella. Inside, there was a note folded twice. The box carried a sentence that read I am the little box that keeps Aunt Nella's seeds. That was true, for the seeds rattled gently within. Each word fit the wood like a key in a pocket. Rainclouds slid away, and Mina laughed. Soon, the craftsperson who made the box came by with plums. On his sleeve, he wore dust from the workshop. For he had carved the lid with a goose and a pear tree. That autumn, he had given the box to Aunt Nella. Her hands had planted sweet beans and marigolds in it. In a scarf fold, she hid the title sentence until she reached the door. She had meant to return the box before supper. So she tucked it under her arm and walked home. The road dipped past the brook and the white cow. Old Mrs Pike waved from her gate. Roses climbed her fence in red tangles. Yonder, the bell in the chapel sang thin and clear. Sunlight found the box and warmed the cedar. Soon, Mina felt as if the little note were singing. Even the hens in the yard paused to listen. Near the door, Aunt Nella peered over her spectacles. Tenderly, she opened the box and smiled. Every bean inside belonged to spring. No one in the village forgot that day. Children came to hear the tale by the hearth. Each asked why the note could speak so plainly. She told them that honest words are light on the tongue. Snow came later, with hard edges on the pond. Pine smoke curled from the chimneys at dusk. Elder Tom brought cider in a jug. Little Mina kept the empty box on her shelf. Later, she wrote her own name under the lid. Then she laughed because it fit so neatly. Her grandmother said a true thing can wear a small coat. In the moonrise, the orchard looked like a silver bowl. Stars shone through the bare branches. That winter, the room smelled of beeswax and pine. Inside, she planed a board for spring. The board would hold new notes for new gifts. Larks would sing before the frost left the grass. Even now, Mina remembers the box and its plain true words.

items.text: Tall cedars shaded the potter's yard at Brindle Hill. Hannah kept the kiln there with her son Milo and a gray cat named Peat. Every morning, villagers brought cracked bowls, dull jugs, and wishes for wedding plates. For each hand she found a fair shape in the clay. In winter, the yard smelled of wet earth and apple smoke. Rainy days sent children under the shed roof to watch the wheel hum. Sometimes Hannah let them press thumbprints into scraps. The smallest thumbprint always belonged to Orra, the shepherd's niece. Last frost, Orra carried in a cup broken clean in two. Even its handle seemed ashamed, hanging by a thread of glaze. The cup had been her mother's, and she feared the sheep bells would sound lonely without it. Tenderly, Hannah set both halves on a cloth. Everyone grew quiet while she mixed slip as pale as cream. Rosy slip gleamed on Hannah's fingers as she worked. Softly, Milo fed chips of pine to the kiln. Outside, the cat guarded the doorway from sparrows. From a shelf, Hannah chose a narrow iron point. Then she mended the cup so neatly that Orra forgot to sniffle. Hannah promised a small gift besides, if Orra could wait until moonrise. In the workshop, she shaped a lid no larger than a plum. She brushed it blue, the color of dusk after rain. Soon the kiln glowed like a loaf with fire in its crust. Through the long afternoon, neighbors came and went with gossip and warm bread. Orra stayed, drowsy but hopeful, counting swallows in the eaves. Red light filled the yard when Hannah drew out the little cup. Yet the gift was not finished, for the lid still held a secret. She cooled it in a basin and rubbed away a bead of ash. Small signs ran around its rim, tidy as seeds in a row. Even Milo bent close, though he had helped with the firing. No one could read them at first, not even the schoolmaster passing by. Then Hannah turned the lid slowly in Orra's hands. Each sign gave the next word of a plain saying. Now Orra read aloud, and her cheeks shone. Come home whole, little cup, and keep the lamb girl merry. Everyone laughed, for that was just what the cup had done. Still, Hannah winked and tapped the rim. Some village craftsperson may be shy, she said, but a shy craft may speak truly. Peat sneezed at the smoke, which made the children cheer. Every bowl on the shelf seemed to sit taller. Later, Orra carried the cup across the pasture with both hands. Lambs gathered near her knees, nosing the blue lid. That night, she poured milk into the mended cup and shared it with Milo. Hannah watched from the door, pleased as a hearth in snow. In the rim she hid the title sentence, though Orra only knew it as a blessing. So the cup kept telling exactly what it was. The village trusted Hannah more after that, not because she boasted. Instead, each pot left her yard with honest clay, honest fire, and a word that fit. To this day, when a child breaks a treasure, the family brings the pieces up Brindle Hill. Little Peat's grandkitten sits by the path and blinks at sparrows. Every repaired cup goes home with its own true saying.

One rainy noon, Mara, who sold papers from a satchel, found the lantern unlit though the train from Fenmere was due. Moss was mending his bootlace, so he told her that a light is fed by little kindnesses. While the rain drummed, he said, she would learn where to look.

Once it was told.
In the harbor town of Grey Quay, old Mara kept a net with three bright knots and a kettle that sang on the stove. On wet mornings she walked the dock with a careful step, and the children followed, hoping for a crumb and a story.
Once it was told.
At dawn, Mara found a boy with salt on his sleeves, and she taught him to knot rope without tugging too hard.
Once it was told.
This is the smallest matter.
So the telling returns.
When the boy smiled, she tied the last knot herself and waved him on.
Once it was told.
At dusk, she set a warm loaf on the sill for the ferryman who had no supper.
This is the smallest matter.
So the telling returns.
The boy took the loaf with both hands, and the gulls quieted on the rail.
So the telling returns.
The grandson listened, and he kept the loose rope coiled by the post.
Once it was told.
Later, when the rain moved inland, she led her granddaughter under the awning and showed her how to dry lantern glass with a soft sleeve.
Once it was told.
This is the smallest matter.
So the telling returns.
The girl tucked the cloth away and kept her balance while the wind worried the ropes.
Once it was told.
After that, she shared a cup of tea with a widow who had lost her gloves to the tide.
This is the smallest matter.
So the telling returns.
And by evening the widow was smiling by the door, warming her hands.
So the telling returns.
And when the sky cleared, Mara laughed, for each small kindness had found its way home again.
So the telling returns.

Once it was told.
At Briar Halt, where gorse leaned over the fence and sheep nibbled the bank, old Porter Moss kept a brass lantern polished like a winter star. One rainy noon, Mara, who sold papers from a satchel, found the lantern unlit though the train from Fenmere was due. Moss was mending his bootlace, so he told her that a light is fed by little kindnesses. While the rain drummed, he said, she would learn where to look.
Once it was told.
Moss spoke of Ada Bell, the keeper of the waiting room, who kept a kettle near the coal stove and a tin of buttons on the sill. When fog hid the fields, she said that no traveler was too small to help a train arrive safe and cheerful.
Once it was told.
At the far bench, Nelly found a red mitten under the timetable board. She tucked a barley sweet inside it and pinned it where the porter would see.
This is the smallest matter.
By tea-time, a shy boy claimed it with a grin.
So the telling returns.
Ada smiled, stirred the coals, and sent Nelly to warm her toes.
Once it was told.
Near the parcel barrow, Tom lifted a fallen label from a crate of hens. He tied it fast with twine and whispered to the birds till they settled.
This is the smallest matter.
The farmer later left him a feather, striped brown and gold.
So the telling returns.
Then Ada poured tea for Moss, and the fog thinned enough for the signal lamp to gleam.
So the telling returns.
Mara looked toward the rain-silvered rails, but the lantern still waited dark. Moss nodded to the ticket hatch and said there was more in the station than brass and wick.
Once it was told.
Moss spoke of Jem Pike, the mender of clocks, who came each Thursday with oil in his pocket and songs under his breath. He believed every tick liked company, and even a cracked face could keep good time if someone cared.
Once it was told.
On the platform stool, Elsie saw a beetle struggling in a saucer of spilled milk. She slid a card beneath it and set it among dry crumbs by the wall.
This is the smallest matter.

Jem wound the clock and let Elsie hold the tiny key.
Once it was told.
Beside the bookstall, Arun found a loose screw from the news rack. He placed it in the bookseller's palm before any wheel could snag a sleeve.
This is the smallest matter.
The bookseller gave him the first look at a comic.
So the telling returns.
Then Jem tapped the clockcase, and its hands met the hour just as a whistle sounded beyond the rain.
So the telling returns.
Mara understood. She took a dry rag, wiped the lantern glass, trimmed the wick with Moss's little scissors, and sheltered the flame while he struck the match. The lamp bloomed amber. The Fenmere train sighed in, bright windows sliding past wet sleepers, and every passenger saw the glow. Moss set one warm bun in Mara's satchel and said that a great light often begins with a deed small enough to fit in a hand.
So the telling returns.

options.C: Dawn wind stirred Mara's little bakery door. The wind carried flour across warm tiles. Old Tomas laughed, chasing wind with brooms. Children smelled wind, sugar, yeast, and cinnamon. Mara told the wind, Behave until breakfast. Even the brick oven hummed with wind. Then one blue bun rose from empty dough. The wind went quiet around Mara's hands. She gave wind a crusty golden roll. Soon wind shared crumbs with every sparrow. Tomas named wind the blue bun's godfather. Mara baked while wind guarded the doorway.

options.A: Morning wind woke Pippa by the bakery. She fed the wind with dry pinecones. Old Bran shaped buns as wind hummed. Wind powdered flour across every wooden sill. Customers laughed, following wind to breakfast early. Pippa promised wind a brown crusty heel. But one round loaf sat still, pale, unsung. Wind tugged aprons, yet that loaf waited. Bran touched it; wind hushed gently outside. Pippa split it, and wind smelled honey. Inside, wind found a sleeping golden bee. So wind carried sweetness through Bellmarket's lanes.

items.text:
Mara lived on a windy hill where three apple trees leaned over a stone wall. Her grandmother showed her how to tuck a pip into dark soil and pat it twice, not for luck, but for kindness.

Round and round again one person.

That person was Mara, and she watered the little twig from a blue cup each morning. When frost silvered the grass, she wrapped the stem in wool from an old mitten and sang to it before school.

Round and round again, one family carried baskets under apple trees together.

By midsummer the young tree gave six small apples, sharp and bright. Mara's mother baked them with oats, her father mended the fence, and her brothers set bowls on the sill for anyone passing hungry.

Round and round again, one village brought ladders, songs, aprons, and sleepy children to Mara's orchard at dawn, sharing sweet windfalls with travelers gladly.

An old peddler said he had never tasted kinder fruit. He traded three copper pans for a jar of Mara's jam, then told the next inn, and the next mill, and the next far farm.

Round and round again, one kingdom tasted Mara's golden jam at winter feasts, and the smallest spoonful carried news of the hill, the bees, the red gate, and the child who planted a single pip beside her grandmother's well, so all hungry hands could share together in peace.

When Mara grew grey, she gave each visiting child a pip wrapped in brown paper. She told them, Plant it where someone lonely may find shade, and leave a bowl ready on the sill.

Round and round again one person.

Round and round again one family waited by the stove through rain.

Round and round again one person.

Round and round again one family kept the kettle warm through winter.

Round and round again one village heard the baker's cart pass, and children ran out with aprons, apples, and shy laughter to greet it.

Round and round again one kingdom sent the same peddler homeward at dusk, and each time he came back to the market, his pack held a finer cloth, a brighter ribbon, a sweeter loaf, until even the watchman smiled and waved him through the gate with steady blessing.

Mara lived above a cobbler shop where the street smelled of rain, leather, and plum cakes. Her father sewed soles by the window, and Mara swept curls of brown hide into a basket for garden beds.

Round and round again, one person.

The person was Old Tovin, who came in with a split boot and no coin till barley time. Mara stitched it while her father nodded, and she tucked a warm bun in the toe.

Round and round again, one family mended boots, shared soup, and smiled.

That family was the Brindleys, seven in a cottage with blue shutters. When Tovin told them of the bun, they brought Mara a pot of bean soup and patched her father's torn apron with red thread.

Round and round again, one village brought wool, apples, nails, songs, and steady hands, until Mara's small kindness had warmed every doorstep by dusk.

So the miller fixed the shop latch, the baker left seed cakes, the shepherd combed soft wool for winter socks, and children lined their shoes neatly by Mara's bench. Her father laughed for the first time since snowmelt.

Round and round again, one kingdom heard how a cobbler's daughter saved a lamb, lent a shawl, lifted a cart, and taught glad neighbors to pass on help, so bells rang from hill farms to sea towns, and every child kept a crumb for the next hungry bird.

Years later, Mara's sign showed a boot with a bun peeping out. Travelers stopped to ask why, and she only smiled, stitched their soles tight, and sent them away walking kinder than they came.

items.text:
Mara lived on a windy hill where three apple trees leaned over a stone wall. Her grandmother showed her how to tuck a pip into dark soil and pat it twice, not for luck, but for kindness.

Round and round again one person.

That person was Mara, and she watered the little twig from a blue cup each morning. When frost silvered the grass, she wrapped the stem in wool from an old mitten and sang to it before school.

Round and round again, one family carried baskets under apple trees together.

By midsummer the young tree gave six small apples, sharp and bright. Mara's mother baked them with oats, her father mended the fence, and her brothers set bowls on the sill for anyone passing hungry.

Round and round again, one village brought ladders, songs, aprons, and sleepy children to Mara's orchard at dawn, sharing sweet windfalls with travelers gladly.

An old peddler said he had never tasted kinder fruit. He traded three copper pans for a jar of Mara's jam, then told the next inn, and the next mill, and the next far farm.

Round and round again, one kingdom tasted Mara's golden jam at winter feasts, and the smallest spoonful carried news of the hill, the bees, the red gate, and the child who planted a single pip beside her grandmother's well, so all hungry hands could share together in peace.

When Mara grew grey, she gave each visiting child a pip wrapped in brown paper. She told them, Plant it where someone lonely may find shade, and leave a bowl ready on the sill.

Round and round again one family waited by the stove through rain.

Round and round again one village listened while the ferryman sang, and the children carried bread from door to door by the river nearby.

items.text:
Mara lived above a cobbler shop where the street smelled of rain, leather, and plum cakes. Her father sewed soles by the window, and Mara swept curls of brown hide into a basket for garden beds.

Round and round again, one person.

The person was Old Tovin, who came in with a split boot and no coin till barley time. Mara stitched it while her father nodded, and she tucked a warm bun in the toe.

Round and round again, one family mended boots, shared soup, and smiled.

That family was the Brindleys, seven in a cottage with blue shutters. When Tovin told them of the bun, they brought Mara a pot of bean soup and patched her father's torn apron with red thread.

Round and round again, one village brought wool, apples, nails, songs, and steady hands, until Mara's small kindness had warmed every doorstep by dusk.

So the miller fixed the shop latch, the baker left seed cakes, the shepherd combed soft wool for winter socks, and children lined their shoes neatly by Mara's bench. Her father laughed for the first time since snowmelt.

Round and round again, one kingdom heard how a cobbler's daughter saved a lamb, lent a shawl, lifted a cart, and taught glad neighbors to pass on help, so bells rang from hill farms to sea towns, and every child kept a crumb for the next hungry bird.

Years later, Mara's sign showed a boot with a bun peeping out. Travelers stopped to ask why, and she only smiled, stitched their soles tight, and sent them away walking kinder than they came.

items.text: At dawn, wind brushed Tilly's hilltop dairy. Grandmother Mara heard wind rattle milk pails. She told Tilly, wind favors patient hands. Together they churned while wind teased rafters. A brown calf followed wind through clover. Tilly laughed, letting wind cool her forehead. By noon, one blue bowl stood utterly still. Mara carried bread as wind warmed it. Soon wind carried butter's sweetness downhill softly. Neighbors came, thanking wind and kindly Tilly. That evening, wind sang under silver stars. Tilly kept the bowl when wind returned.

At dusk, Mara mended nets beside wind.
Old Tavi said wind guarded the reeds.
Little Jun brought bread to wind tonight.
The fox sat quiet when wind sang.
Grandma Nell laughed, feeling wind in aprons.
She told boats homeward by wind lantern.
Then one goose stayed, pecking all morning alone.
Mara found wind in the willow cradle.
Jun sang soft, and wind kept time.
Even the dog listened while wind hummed.
By moonrise, wind brushed the moor path.
All night, wind watched over their sleep.

Morning wind woke Pippa by the bakery. She fed the wind with dry pinecones. Old Bran shaped buns as wind hummed. Wind powdered flour across every wooden sill. Customers laughed, following wind to breakfast early. Pippa promised wind a brown crusty heel. But one round loaf sat still, pale, unsung. Wind tugged aprons, yet that loaf waited. Bran touched it; wind hushed gently outside. Pippa split it, and wind smelled honey. Inside, wind found a sleeping golden bee. So wind carried sweetness through Bellmarket's lanes.

At Rowan's orchard wind bent every branch. Grandmother said wind kept the pears sweet. By noon wind carried songs across furrows. Eli followed wind to the stone well. Mother laughed, saying wind knew every gate. That evening wind warmed soup beside fire. Old Mara found a bent nail by gate. She tapped the gatepost and wind answered. Eli smiled when wind lifted his cap. Grandmother mended sleeves while wind hummed outside. The orchard slept yet wind watched kindly. At dawn wind brought the children bread.

Dawn wind stirred Mara's little bakery door. The wind carried flour across warm tiles. Old Tomas laughed, chasing wind with brooms. Children smelled wind, sugar, yeast, and cinnamon. Mara told the wind, Behave until breakfast. Even the brick oven hummed with wind. Then one blue bun rose from empty dough. The wind went quiet around Mara's hands. She gave wind a crusty golden roll. Soon wind shared crumbs with every sparrow. Tomas named wind the blue bun's godfather. Mara baked while wind guarded the doorway.

Hairy Ball Theorem (a corollary of Poincaré–Hopf): On every even-dimensional sphere S^{2n} (χ = 2 ≠ 0), every continuous tangent vector field has a zero; moreover, on S² one can construct a tangent vector field with exactly one zero (pull back a constant vector field on the plane by stereographic projection; the unique zero is at the north pole and has index 2). Thus a zero is unavoidable, and it can be realized as the only zero.

items.text: Morning wind woke Pippa by the bakery. She fed the wind with dry pinecones. Old Bran shaped buns as wind hummed. Wind powdered flour across every wooden sill. Customers laughed, following wind to breakfast early. Pippa promised wind a brown crusty heel. But one round loaf sat still, pale, unsung. Wind tugged aprons, yet that loaf waited. Bran touched it; wind hushed gently outside. Pippa split it, and wind smelled honey. Inside, wind found a sleeping golden bee. So wind carried sweetness through Bellmarket's lanes.

items.text: At Rowan's orchard wind bent every branch. Grandmother said wind kept the pears sweet. By noon wind carried songs across furrows. Eli followed wind to the stone well. Mother laughed, saying wind knew every gate. That evening wind warmed soup beside fire. Old Mara found a bent nail by gate. She tapped the gatepost and wind answered. Eli smiled when wind lifted his cap. Grandmother mended sleeves while wind hummed outside. The orchard slept yet wind watched kindly. At dawn wind brought the children bread.

items.text: Dawn wind stirred Mara's little bakery door. The wind carried flour across warm tiles. Old Tomas laughed, chasing wind with brooms. Children smelled wind, sugar, yeast, and cinnamon. Mara told the wind, Behave until breakfast. Even the brick oven hummed with wind. Then one blue bun rose from empty dough. The wind went quiet around Mara's hands. She gave wind a crusty golden roll. Soon wind shared crumbs with every sparrow. Tomas named wind the blue bun's godfather. Mara baked while wind guarded the doorway.

items.text: Mara, 1, tended the old pear orchard beside Briar Brook. Tobin, 2, swept the mossy path because his boots loved neat ground. Again, 3, Mara hung crumbs on the low branch for the robin. Sunup, 4, he tapped the gatepost with his broom. The, 5, baker's boy left a warm roll in Mara's basket. Again, 6, Mara shared half the roll with the robin. Tobin, 7, found a dropped red mitten under the pear roots. Clouds, 8, he tapped the gatepost with his broom. Again, 9, Mara tucked the mitten on a twig to dry. By, 10, noon the schoolchildren came chasing a paper kite. Little, 11, Elspeth cried when the kite snagged high above her. Again, 12, Mara steadied the ladder, he tapped the gatepost with his broom. Down, 13, fluttered the kite and Elspeth laughed through her tears. Mara, 14, gave Tobin the red mitten because his hand was cold. Again, 15, Mara set crumbs out and the robin brought a berry. Evening, 16, he tapped the gatepost with his broom. The, 17, berry stained Mara's thumb as purple as elder wine. Again, 18, Mara laughed and marked Tobin's nose with it. Geese, 19, came grumbling home along the brookside soft grass. Dusk, 20, he tapped the gatepost with his broom. Again, 21, Mara whistled to the robin and heard two answers. Tobin, 22, lifted his cap when one answer came from Elspeth. She, 23, had hidden behind the cider barrel with apples in her apron. Again, 24, Mara opened the gate wide, he tapped the gatepost with his broom.

Customers laughed, following wind to breakfast early. Pippa promised wind a brown crusty heel. But one round loaf sat still, pale, unsung. Wind tugged aprons, yet that loaf waited. Bran touched it; wind hushed gently outside. Pippa split it, and wind smelled honey. Inside, wind found a sleeping golden bee. So wind carried sweetness through Bellmarket's lanes.

options.D: Forgetting the over/under information at each crossing defines a surjective homomorphism \(□ \to S_n\) (\(\sigma_i \mapsto\) the transposition \((i, i+1)\)), which sends each □ to the permutation of its endpoints; its kernel is the pure □ group \(□\) (Artin).

At dusk on River Lane, the miller kept his lamp bright, and the lane smelled of wet reeds and fresh meal.
[Villager A -> the miller] “My little one is hungry, and the porridge pot is bare.”
The miller set aside a white scoop for her and bade her walk home easy.
[the miller -> Villager B] “Take this sack to your mother, and say the stone gave kindly today.”
He tipped his cap and went off with the load on his back.
[Villager C -> the miller] “My boots are soaked, and I would trade this loaf for a few cupfuls.”
The miller smiled, filled the loaf with dry grain, and set it on the counter.
[the miller -> Villager D] “Carry this warm loaf to your uncle, and keep to the dry path by the hedge.”
He tucked it close and thanked the miller twice.
[Villager E -> the miller] “My cart wheel has come loose, and I need a peg before nightfall.”
The miller found a hard peg, and the cart rolled away with a glad heart.

On market day by the stone well, the miller kept a little stool for news, and the folk came to him with their small concerns.
[Villager A -> the miller] “My little comb is lost near the cart.”
[the miller -> Villager B] “Set two loaves on the blue cloth.”
[Villager C -> the miller] “A calf is nosing the turnips again.”
[the miller -> Villager D] “Carry the seed to the shed, please.”
[Villager E -> the miller] “The lamp by the gate needs oil.”
[the miller -> Villager A] “I have found the comb on my shelf.”
Then he gave Villager B a warm heel of bread, sent Villager D home before the rain, and told the children there would be honey cakes at dusk.

On market day, when apples shone in baskets and penny whistles piped by the green, the miller came down the road with flour on his sleeves and kindness in his cap.

Villager A hurried up with cheeks as red as crab apples.

[Villager A -> the miller] “My goose has stolen my blue ribbon.”

The miller bowed as if a goose with finery were serious business, which indeed it was.

[the miller -> Villager B] “Please watch for a goose wearing sky-blue.”

Villager B shaded one eye and peered past the cabbage cart, past the pots of honey, and past three boys sharing a bun.

[Villager B -> the miller] “I saw it by the pear stall.”

The miller thanked him and strolled on, not fast enough to frighten feathers.

[the miller -> Villager C] “Stand gently by your pear baskets and hum.”

Villager C hummed a cradle song so soft that even the pears seemed to listen.

[Villager C -> the miller] “The goose likes humming and has come close.”

The goose waddled nearer, proud as a mayor, the blue ribbon trailing from its beak.

[the miller -> Villager D] “Fetch the little net from your fish barrow.”

Villager D brought the net folded over both hands, with not a hook or thorn upon it.

[Villager D -> the miller] “Here is the net, soft as a cobweb.”

The miller laid it low in the grass, then took a crust from his pocket and thought better of it.

[the miller -> Villager E] “Bring a crust from your basket and smile.”

Villager E came with bread still warm from home, and the goose forgot its grandeur for supper.

[Villager E -> the miller] “The goose follows crumbs like a prince.”

So the miller caught the ribbon, not the goose, and the goose kept its dignity.

[the miller -> Villager A] “Tie your ribbon and thank the goose kindly.”

Villager A tied the ribbon round her hat, gave the goose the last crumb, and all the market laughed as warmly as a kettle sings.

options.A: Classic application (Erdős's favorite warm-up problem, instantly solved by the young Pósa over dinner): among any n+1 integers chosen from {1, ..., 2n}, one divides another. Proof: every integer can be written uniquely as 2^t m with m odd, and there are exactly n odd numbers in {1, ..., 2n}; hence there are only n possible odd parts. Choosing n+1 integers, two must have the same odd part, so their quotient is a power of 2, and therefore the smaller divides the larger.
options.B: Newman’s lemma (1942): a terminating (strongly normalizing) abstract rewriting system that is locally □ is globally □; hence, for every element, all of its reduction sequences end in the same unique normal form. options.C: A tree of diameter 2 is necessarily \(K_{1,n}\) (\(n\ge2\)); moreover, among all trees on \(n+1\) vertices, \(K_{1,n}\) uniquely attains the minimum Wiener index \(W(K_{1,n})=n^2\) (Entringer–Jackson–Snyder 1976: among trees, the Wiener index is minimized by \(K_{1,n}\) and maximized by the path graph).

Corollary: If u and v are connected and nonadjacent, then all paths between u and v □ if and only if this maximum number is 1.

[the miller -> Villager B] “Take this fresh loaf”

[Villager E -> the miller] “Thank you kindly”
By evening, the wheel was quiet, and the neighbors went home with bread and cheer.

At dusk on River Lane, the miller kept his lamp bright, and the lane smelled of wet reeds and fresh meal.
[Villager A -> the miller] “My little one is hungry, and the porridge pot is bare.”
The miller set aside a white scoop for her and bade her walk home easy.
[the miller -> Villager B] “Take this sack to your mother, and say the stone gave kindly today.”
He tipped his cap and went off with the load on his back.
[Villager C -> the miller] “My boots are soaked, and I would trade this loaf for a few cupfuls.”
The miller smiled, filled the loaf with dry grain, and set it on the counter.
[the miller -> Villager D] “Carry this warm loaf to your uncle, and keep to the dry path by the hedge.”
He tucked it close and thanked the miller twice.
[Villager E -> the miller] “My cart wheel has come loose, and I need a peg before nightfall.”
The miller found a hard peg, and the cart rolled away with a glad heart.

On market day by the stone well, the miller kept a little stool for news, and the folk came to him with their small concerns.
[Villager A -> the miller] “My little comb is lost near the cart.”
[the miller -> Villager B] “Set two loaves on the blue cloth.”
[Villager C -> the miller] “A calf is nosing the turnips again.”
[the miller -> Villager D] “Carry the seed to the shed, please.”
[Villager E -> the miller] “The lamp by the gate needs oil.”
[the miller -> Villager A] “I have found the comb on my shelf.”
Then he gave Villager B a warm heel of bread, sent Villager D home before the rain, and told the children there would be honey cakes at dusk.

On market day, when apples shone in baskets and penny whistles piped by the green, the miller came down the road with flour on his sleeves and kindness in his cap.

Villager A hurried up with cheeks as red as crab apples.

[Villager A -> the miller] “My goose has stolen my blue ribbon.”

The miller bowed as if a goose with finery were serious business, which indeed it was.

[the miller -> Villager B] “Please watch for a goose wearing sky-blue.”

Villager B shaded one eye and peered past the cabbage cart, past the pots of honey, and past three boys sharing a bun.

[Villager B -> the miller] “I saw it by the pear stall.”

The miller thanked him and strolled on, not fast enough to frighten feathers.

[the miller -> Villager C] “Stand gently by your pear baskets and hum.”

Villager C hummed a cradle song so soft that even the pears seemed to listen.

[Villager C -> the miller] “The goose likes humming and has come close.”

The goose waddled nearer, proud as a mayor, the blue ribbon trailing from its beak.

[the miller -> Villager D] “Fetch the little net from your fish barrow.”

Villager D brought the net folded over both hands, with not a hook or thorn upon it.

[Villager D -> the miller] “Here is the net, soft as a cobweb.”

The miller laid it low in the grass, then took a crust from his pocket and thought better of it.

[the miller -> Villager E] “Bring a crust from your basket and smile.”

Villager E came with bread still warm from home, and the goose forgot its grandeur for supper.

[Villager E -> the miller] “The goose follows crumbs like a prince.”

So the miller caught the ribbon, not the goose, and the goose kept its dignity.

[the miller -> Villager A] “Tie your ribbon and thank the goose kindly.”

Villager A tied the ribbon round her hat, gave the goose the last crumb, and all the market laughed as warmly as a kettle sings.

Holder 9 says, under the elder's carved chair, he points to Holder 5 for the shuttle, the wool wrap, and the right to keep them. At a round table sat eight people, labeled 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7, and one lamp lay warm on the cloth.
gcd(3,8)=1
"Each time, skip 2 people and hand the lamp to the 3rd person."
The lamp went 0, 3, 6, 1, 4, 7, 2, 5, 0.
An elder smiled and said, "Three and eight are coprime, so the lamp misses no one."
Then, by the same fire, the elder tried again.
gcd(2,8)=2
"Each time, skip 1 person and hand the lamp to the 2nd person."
The lamp went 0, 2, 4, 6, 0, 2, 4, 6, 0.
The people who never receive the lamp are 1, 3, 5, 7.

At a round table in the orchard sat 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and there was one lamp beside a bowl of apples. They said, "Each time, skip 2 people and hand the lamp to the 3rd person." For the □ group \mathbb{Z}_n, an element k generates \mathbb{Z}_n if and only if \gcd(k,n)=1, so \mathbb{Z}_n has exactly \varphi(n) generators (Euler's totient function, Euler 1763; theorem in Gallian's Contemporary Abstract Algebra, Thm. 4.2 and its corollary). Systematic study of the star polygons \{n/k\} appears in Poinsot (1810). Musical example: in the 12-tone system, a step of 7 (a perfect fifth) because \gcd(7,12)=1 traverses all twelve pitch classes and returns to the starting point—the circle of fifths.

options.A: Orbit Lemma (a corollary of the □ principle): let |X| = n and f: X → X. For any initial value x, the first n + 1 terms of the sequence x, f(x), f²(x), … must contain a repetition, so the orbit eventually falls into a pure □ of length p ≤ n. In particular, when f is a bijection, its functional graph decomposes exactly into disjoint directed □ (the □ decomposition theorem for permutations).
options.B: For the □ group \mathbb{Z}_n, an element k generates \mathbb{Z}_n if and only if \gcd(k,n)=1, so \mathbb{Z}_n has exactly \varphi(n) generators (Euler's totient function, Euler 1763; theorem in Gallian's Contemporary Abstract Algebra, Thm. 4.2 and its corollary). Systematic study of the star polygons \{n/k\} appears in Poinsot (1810). Musical example: in the 12-tone system, a step of 7 (a perfect fifth) because \gcd(7,12)=1 traverses all twelve pitch classes and returns to the starting point—the circle of fifths.
options.C: Classic application (Erdős's favorite warm-up problem, instantly solved by the young Pósa over dinner): among any n+1 integers chosen from {1, ..., 2n}, one divides another. Proof: every integer can be written uniquely as 2^t m with m odd, and there are exactly n odd numbers in {1, ..., 2n}; hence there are only n possible odd parts. Choosing n+1 integers, two must have the same odd part, so their quotient is a power of 2, and therefore the smaller divides the larger.
options.D: If f has positive integer period p and g has positive integer period q, then lcm(p,q) is a period of f+g (not necessarily the least). When gcd(p,q) = 1, the phase pair (n mod p, n mod q) runs through all pq combinations exactly once every pq steps as n advances, returning to (0,0) (by the Chinese remainder theorem); hence the two patterns are □ only once every pq steps.

At a round table sat eight people, labeled 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7, and one lamp lay warm on the cloth.
gcd(3,8)=1
"Each time, skip 2 people and hand the lamp to the 3rd person."
The lamp went 0, 3, 6, 1, 4, 7, 2, 5, 0.
An elder smiled and said, "Three and eight are coprime, so the lamp misses no one."
Then, by the same fire, the elder tried again.
gcd(2,8)=2
"Each time, skip 1 person and hand the lamp to the 2nd person."

options.A: If f has positive integer period p and g has positive integer period q, then lcm(p,q) is a period of f+g (not necessarily the least). When gcd(p,q) = 1, the phase pair (n mod p, n mod q) runs through all pq combinations exactly once every pq steps as n advances, returning to (0,0) (by the Chinese remainder theorem); hence the two patterns are □ only once every pq steps.
options.B: Orbit Lemma (a corollary of the □ principle): let |X| = n and f: X → X. For any initial value x, the first n + 1 terms of the sequence x, f(x), f²(x), … must contain a repetition, so the orbit eventually falls into a pure □ of length p ≤ n. In particular, when f is a bijection, its functional graph decomposes exactly into disjoint directed □ (the □ decomposition theorem for permutations).

Mara the baker rose before dawn, when the oven bricks still held last night’s warmth and the lane smelled of rain.

On the flour table stood twelve painted boxes, one label apiece: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December.

By sunrise, thirteen travelers came in from the wet road for oatcakes and honey. Mara tied card tags to their cloaks, and the tags read: Traveler 1, Traveler 2, Traveler 3, Traveler 4, Traveler 5, Traveler 6, Traveler 7, Traveler 8, Traveler 9, Traveler 10, Traveler 11, Traveler 12, Traveler 13.

Above the bread shelf hung the bakehouse rule: "Every traveler belongs to exactly one birth month."

Old Nessa, who had sugared buns since Mara was small, wiped her hands on her apron and said, "Thirteen is more than twelve, so at least two travelers were born in the same month."

The children laughed and peered at the boxes, but Nessa would not point. “Let the cards tell it when the tea is poured,” she said.

So they ate. Crumbs fell like tiny snow. The kettle sang, boots dried by the hearth, and Mara wrote each answer on a clean white page.

At dusk she unrolled the page beside the boxes:

Nella was the Weaver of Wrenford Green, and the Loom stood beside the schoolyard with a blue door and a bell of tin.
Each morning, Nella fed thread through careful fingers, set the shuttle in motion with a soft clack, and hummed for the sparrows in the eaves.

Nella moved the cloth aside, set a bowl of broth by the Loom, and waited until the little paws stopped knocking.

Telling One:
Nella was the Weaver of Wrenford Green, and the Loom stood beside the schoolyard with a blue door and a bell of tin.
Each morning, Nella fed thread through careful fingers, set the shuttle in motion with a soft clack, and hummed for the sparrows in the eaves.
One wet Friday, a small fox crept in, shivering so hard that the cloth on the counter stirred.
Nella moved the cloth aside, set a bowl of broth by the Loom, and waited until the little paws stopped knocking.
By sunset the fox nosed a lost silver thimble from under the step, so Nella hung it on the blue door for luck.

items.text: At the hill orchard, old Mara kept two baskets of stones, broad yellow ones and slim blue ones. "Pick kindly, Tom." Tom set a yellow stone by the gate, and its nick kissed the notch of a blue stone. All morning the children added stones wherever the little marks agreed, leaving no bare earth between roots. "This one remembers me." By noon, every path seemed familiar, yet no path lay just where Tom expected it. "Seen before, never same." Mara laughed softly and showed him how a broad stone often found more broad cousins than slim ones. Still, the slim stones were never lonely, for each held a corner that called another child closer. "No place is the master." They walked from pear trees to bee hives, and every small handful of stones came again soon. But the whole orchard refused to slide into its earlier self, however far Tom dragged his gaze. "Then it is alive." A blackbird hopped over the joins, finding every edge snug, every crossing tidy, every crumb of soil covered. "Nothing is lost here." When evening cooled the ladders, Mara counted their baskets and smiled at the yellow stones left fewer. Tom counted the laid stones instead, and found yellow ahead of blue by a pleasing handful. "Tomorrow, bring the neighbors." So next day more hands came, and each new child could begin anywhere without mending a mistake. "Where does it end?" Mara pointed past the last apple tree, where grass waited, and Tom carried two stones onward.

At Mossford washhouse, Lina kept two rubbing stones, one broad as a bun and one slim as a fish. "Mind the corners," Nana said. Each dawn, folk brought shirts, shawls, and baby blankets, and Lina set the stones wherever cloth seemed most needful. The broad stone loved wide muddy patches, while the slim stone slipped into cuffs, collars, and places fingers missed. "No gap for dirt," Lina laughed. She worked across every heap with quiet care, setting broad beside slim whenever the linen asked. "Seen that sleeve before," piped Tom. Lina winked, for a blue cuff would turn up near the tub, then by the door, never just where expected. By noon the benches lay covered edge to edge with clean cloth, yet no row looked like another. "How do you remember?" asked Mara. Lina tapped her brow, then chose a broad stone for the apron and a slim one for the torn kerchief. Every stain found a neighbor, every corner found a hand, and the suds ran clear through the drain. "Tea first," declared old Reuben. They ate oatcakes on the steps, watching steam rise from shirts spread over lavender bushes and willow rails. "That mark appears," Mara whispered. Lina showed her three yellow socks apart, each mended with red thread, each lodged among different whites. Before sunset, the whole green smelled of soap, rainwater, and thyme, with garments touching from pump to fence. "Nothing sits alone," said Nana. When a wind lifted one sheet, children saw another tucked near it, not twin, but kin enough to comfort. "And nowhere the same," Tom smiled. So Mossford slept under fresh linen, and Lina's two stones rested together, having made a village bright without making it plain.

At dusk, Mara and her grandmother carried a basket of blue crumbs, bread, and onions to the lane beside the mill. "Set the first stone gently," said Grandmother. The mason's yard held two kinds of flat stones, one broad as a palm, the other slim as a finger, and both were cool with rain. He fitted each one by little nicks on its edge, so the next would sit kindly beside it without a wobble. "That one's for the door," whispered Mara. By morning, the courtyard spread out behind the shop like a pale rug, and the hens picked grain from the seams between the stones. "Do not force it," he said. When a child dragged a heel, the little edge caught, and the mason smiled, because the stones welcomed only careful feet. At supper, the widow told how traders once brought these stones from a far hill where goats rang their bells. "Count them by hand," said the child. Mara counted broad to slim, then slim to broad, and the tally kept drifting, though every row looked kindly set. No straight shove of the board made the whole yard look alike, yet every corner found its mate with ease. "Leave the chalk line," said Nan. By lantern light, the floor seemed shy and lively at once, as if each stone knew its neighbor's habits and kept them. "This one turns there," murmured Mara. She laid a pebble at the threshold, and a copper cup on the sill, while her grandmother hummed a harvest tune. Soon the courtyard held no empty place, yet the eye could wander from patch to patch and never meet a weary break. "See how it welcomes rain," said Nan. When storm water came, it ran in bright threads, then slipped away, and the stones stayed firm under the feet of all who crossed. "Bring the lamp closer," said Mara. At the last glow, the old mason nodded from the doorway, and the children knew the yard would keep its quiet welcome.

On the hill above the bakery, Mara sorted two baskets of flat stones while the oven breathed warm bread through the door.
"Set the broad one here," said Tamsin.
Mara set it beside a slim one, and the join sat neat enough to please her careful eye.
By noon, the yard held a winding strip of pale and dark stones that nobody could have guessed from the first basket.
"A little more," whispered Mara.
An old cat slept on the flour sacks, and the men carrying yeast glanced over as if the ground were telling a joke.
"No gaps," said Tamsin.
So Mara tucked each stone to the next one, turning a broad piece when a narrow one would not sit kindly.
When the rain came, it washed the dust clean, and the wet shine made the whole yard seem newly blessed.
"Keep going," said Eli.
At supper, Mara counted thirteen broad slabs and eight slim ones, then smiled at the tidy sum.
She had not set them by rule book, only by the feel of a stone meeting its neighbors under her thumbs.
"Pretty work," said the miller.
Children from the lane came to hop across the dry places, and each one found a fresh way home.
"Again tomorrow," cried Nell.
Mara laughed, because tomorrow would bring more baskets, more hands, and the steady good patience in her palms.
Long after dark, the lantern near the door threw gold across the stones, and not one line of it held still.
"Sleep well," said Tamsin.
The next market day, travelers paused, and some swore they had seen the lane before, though none could name where.
"There it is," murmured Mara.
By the time the last loaf cooled, the bakery yard held its quiet blessing, and every footstep found its place.

On the harbor lane, old Mara kept two kinds of floor stones in a blue apron, broad ones and slim ones, and the children gathered to see what she would do with them. "Take one," she said. She laid them by a plain rule: each stone asked for the next kind beside it, and every child who helped could learn it after one careful look. When the sun slid across the boards, the floor grew calm and full, with no bare places left for dust or boot heels to complain about. "Mind the seams," said Ben. Mara smiled, because the seams fit so cleanly that even a mouse could not find a crooked step anywhere along the lane. "Again," whispered Nell. So the little hands went on, and the floor kept growing under them, one choice at a time, until it shone like a pond at dusk. By supper, the boys and girls could point to any small patch of stones and find it again elsewhere, yet never with the road shifted under their feet. "There," said Mara. The neighbors called it a kindly road, because it welcomed carts, rainwater, and bare toes without ever asking to be dressed in another way. Years later, travelers still found the same snug corner for a rest, and the children laughed to see how the floor remembered their feet. "Easy now," said Tom. No one could slide the whole floor a single step and make it match itself, not the dockmaster, not the miller, not even Mara with her strong hands. "See," she said. Still, if a baby dropped a crumb or a sailor lost a button, some kind hand would find an old likeness nearby before long, as if the lane kept good memory for small things. That was why the folk came from far off to sweep the stones with their eyes, and they went home lighter, as though they had heard a cradle song from the ground. "Good night," said the miller. At dawn, the first gulls found no end to the kindness of the lane, only more quiet places where a step could rest and go on. "Come back," sang Mara. So the harbor children grew up trusting that a road may be kind without ever going dull, and they carried that lesson into every house they built.

items.text: At the hill orchard, old Mara kept two baskets of stones, broad yellow ones and slim blue ones. "Pick kindly, Tom." Tom set a yellow stone by the gate, and its nick kissed the notch of a blue stone. All morning the children added stones wherever the little marks agreed, leaving no bare earth between roots. "This one remembers me." By noon, every path seemed familiar, yet no path lay just where Tom expected it. "Seen before, never same." Mara laughed softly and showed him how a broad stone often found more broad cousins than slim ones. Still, the slim stones were never lonely, for each held a corner that called another child closer. "No place is the master." They walked from pear trees to bee hives, and every small handful of stones came again soon. But the whole orchard refused to slide into its earlier self, however far Tom dragged his gaze. "Then it is alive." A blackbird hopped over the joins, finding every edge snug, every crossing tidy, every crumb of soil covered. "Nothing is lost here." When evening cooled the ladders, Mara counted their baskets and smiled at the yellow stones left fewer. Tom counted the laid stones instead, and found yellow ahead of blue by a pleasing handful. "Tomorrow, bring the neighbors." So next day more hands came, and each new child could begin anywhere without mending a mistake. "Where does it end?" Mara pointed past the last apple tree, where grass waited, and Tom carried two stones onward.

items.text: At Mossford washhouse, Lina kept two rubbing stones, one broad as a bun and one slim as a fish. "Mind the corners," Nana said. Each dawn, folk brought shirts, shawls, and baby blankets, and Lina set the stones wherever cloth seemed most needful. The broad stone loved wide muddy patches, while the slim stone slipped into cuffs, collars, and places fingers missed. "No gap for dirt," Lina laughed. She worked across every heap with quiet care, setting broad beside slim whenever the linen asked. "Seen that sleeve before," piped Tom. Lina winked, for a blue cuff would turn up near the tub, then by the door, never just where expected. By noon the benches lay covered edge to edge with clean cloth, yet no row looked like another. "How do you remember?" asked Mara. Lina tapped her brow, then chose a broad stone for the apron and a slim one for the torn kerchief. Every stain found a neighbor, every corner found a hand, and the suds ran clear through the drain. "Tea first," declared old Reuben. They ate oatcakes on the steps, watching steam rise from shirts spread over lavender bushes and willow rails. "That mark appears," Mara whispered. Lina showed her three yellow socks apart, each mended with red thread, each lodged among different whites. Before sunset, the whole green smelled of soap, rainwater, and thyme, with garments touching from pump to fence. "Nothing sits alone," said Nana. When a wind lifted one sheet, children saw another tucked near it, not twin, but kin enough to comfort. "And nowhere the same," Tom smiled. So Mossford slept under fresh linen, and Lina's two stones rested together, having made a village bright without making it plain.

items.text: At dusk, Mara and her grandmother carried a basket of blue crumbs, bread, and onions to the lane beside the mill. "Set the first stone gently," said Grandmother. The mason's yard held two kinds of flat stones, one broad as a palm, the other slim as a finger, and both were cool with rain. He fitted each one by little nicks on its edge, so the next would sit kindly beside it without a wobble. "That one's for the door," whispered Mara. By morning, the courtyard spread out behind the shop like a pale rug, and the hens picked grain from the seams between the stones. "Do not force it," he said. When a child dragged a heel, the little edge caught, and the mason smiled, because the stones welcomed only careful feet. At supper, the widow told how traders once brought these stones from a far hill where goats rang their bells. "Count them by hand," said the child. Mara counted broad to slim, then slim to broad, and the tally kept drifting, though every row looked kindly set. No straight shove of the board made the whole yard look alike, yet every corner found its mate with ease. "Leave the chalk line," said Nan. By lantern light, the floor seemed shy and lively at once, as if each stone knew its neighbor's habits and kept them. "This one turns there," murmured Mara. She laid a pebble at the threshold, and a copper cup on the sill, while her grandmother hummed a harvest tune. Soon the courtyard held no empty place, yet the eye could wander from patch to patch and never meet a weary break. "See how it welcomes rain," said Nan. When storm water came, it ran in bright threads, then slipped away, and the stones stayed firm under the feet of all who crossed. "Bring the lamp closer," said Mara. At the last glow, the old mason nodded from the doorway, and the children knew the yard would keep its quiet welcome.

On the hill above the bakery, Mara sorted two baskets of flat stones while the oven breathed warm bread through the door.
"Set the broad one here," said Tamsin.
Mara set it beside a slim one, and the join sat neat enough to please her careful eye.
By noon, the yard held a winding strip of pale and dark stones that nobody could have guessed from the first basket.
"A little more," whispered Mara.
An old cat slept on the flour sacks, and the men carrying yeast glanced over as if the ground were telling a joke.
"No gaps," said Tamsin.
So Mara tucked each stone to the next one, turning a broad piece when a narrow one would not sit kindly.
When the rain came, it washed the dust clean, and the wet shine made the whole yard seem newly blessed.
"Keep going," said Eli.
At supper, Mara counted thirteen broad slabs and eight slim ones, then smiled at the tidy sum.
She had not set them by rule book, only by the feel of a stone meeting its neighbors under her thumbs.
"Pretty work," said the miller.
Children from the lane came to hop across the dry places, and each one found a fresh way home.
"Again tomorrow," cried Nell.
Mara laughed, because tomorrow would bring more baskets, more hands, and the steady good patience in her palms.
Long after dark, the lantern near the door threw gold across the stones, and not one line of it held still.
"Sleep well," said Tamsin.
The next market day, travelers paused, and some swore they had seen the lane before, though none could name where.
"There it is," murmured Mara.
By the time the last loaf cooled, the bakery yard held its quiet blessing, and every footstep found its place.

items.text: On the harbor lane, old Mara kept two kinds of floor stones in a blue apron, broad ones and slim ones, and the children gathered to see what she would do with them. "Take one," she said. She laid them by a plain rule: each stone asked for the next kind beside it, and every child who helped could learn it after one careful look. When the sun slid across the boards, the floor grew calm and full, with no bare places left for dust or boot heels to complain about. "Mind the seams," said Ben. Mara smiled, because the seams fit so cleanly that even a mouse could not find a crooked step anywhere along the lane. "Again," whispered Nell. So the little hands went on, and the floor kept growing under them, one choice at a time, until it shone like a pond at dusk. By supper, the boys and girls could point to any small patch of stones and find it again elsewhere, yet never with the road shifted under their feet. "There," said Mara. The neighbors called it a kindly road, because it welcomed carts, rainwater, and bare toes without ever asking to be dressed in another way. Years later, travelers still found the same snug corner for a rest, and the children laughed to see how the floor remembered their feet. "Easy now," said Tom. No one could slide the whole floor a single step and make it match itself, not the dockmaster, not the miller, not even Mara with her strong hands. "See," she said. Still, if a baby dropped a crumb or a sailor lost a button, some kind hand would find an old likeness nearby before long, as if the lane kept good memory for small things. That was why the folk came from far off to sweep the stones with their eyes, and they went home lighter, as though they had heard a cradle song from the ground. "Good night," said the miller. At dawn, the first gulls found no end to the kindness of the lane, only more quiet places where a step could rest and go on. "Come back," sang Mara. So the harbor children grew up trusting that a road may be kind without ever going dull, and they carried that lesson into every house they built.
